stem: How must an ammeter be connected in a circuit to measure the electric current through a component?

options.text: In series with the component, so that all of the current flows through it.
In parallel with the power supply, so that it shares the current equally with all components.
In series after the component, because current only flows up to the point of a break.
In parallel across the component, so that it measures the current flowing through it.

rationale: An ammeter must be connected in series with a component so that all of the current flows through the meter.

evidence.quote: An ammeter must be connected in series with the component, so that all of the current flows through it.

stem: A student sets up a circuit loop containing a cell, a switch, and a lamp. If a wire breaks between the switch and the lamp, what happens to the electric current in the circuit?

options.text: The current stops flowing in the whole loop immediately.
The current continues to flow through the wire up to the point of the break.
The current increases in the unbroken part of the circuit to make up for the break.
The current flows from the positive terminal up to the break, then moves backward.

rationale: Current requires a complete circuit to flow, so a break anywhere in the loop stops the current in the entire loop.

evidence.quote: A break anywhere in the loop stops the current in the whole loop.

stem: A current of 0.5 A flows through a resistor for 20 seconds. How much charge passes through the resistor, and from which terminal do the electrons originate?

options.text: 10 C of charge passes through, with electrons moving from the positive terminal.
0.025 C of charge passes through, with electrons moving from the negative terminal.
10 C of charge passes through, with electrons moving from the negative terminal.
40 C of charge passes through, measured by an ammeter connected in parallel.

rationale: The charge is calculated using Q = I × t = 0.5 A × 20 s = 10 C, and electrons move from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.

evidence.quote: The formula is I = Q / t, where I is the current in amperes (A), Q is the charge in coulombs (C) and t is the time in seconds (s).

stem: An electric component has a current of 1 ampere flowing through it. What does a current of one ampere mean in terms of charge?

options.text: One joule of energy is transferred to each coulomb of charge per second.
One coulomb of charge passes through an ammeter connected in parallel.
One coulomb of charge passes a point every second.
One coulomb of charge flows per second up to any break in the wire.

rationale: A current of one ampere is defined as one coulomb of charge passing a point every second.

evidence.quote: A current of one ampere means that one coulomb of charge passes a point every second.

stem: What is electric current?

options.text: The movement of electrons from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
The opposition of a material to the flow of moving charges.
The flow of electric charge through a conductor.
The flow of electric charge that moves up to the point of a break in a wire.

rationale: Electric current is defined as the flow of electric charge through a conductor.

evidence.quote: Electric current is the flow of electric charge through a conductor.

stem: How must a voltmeter be connected in a circuit to measure the potential difference across a component?

options.text: In series, so potential difference can flow through it.
In parallel with the switch, before current enters it.
In parallel, across the component being measured.
In series, in line with the component being measured.

rationale: A voltmeter is always connected in parallel across a component to measure the potential difference between two points.

evidence.quote: A voltmeter must be connected in parallel, across the component being measured.

stem: Which statement correctly describes potential difference in an electric circuit?

options.text: It is the fixed total amount of energy given to a circuit by a battery.
It is the rate at which electric charge passes a given point per second.
It is the energy transferred per coulomb of charge between two points.
It is a physical quantity that flows through the wires alongside current.

rationale: Potential difference is defined as the amount of energy transferred to or from each coulomb of charge passing between two points.

evidence.quote: Potential difference (voltage) between two points is the energy transferred to or from each coulomb of charge as it moves between those points.

stem: A cell with a potential difference of 12 V moves 4 C of charge through a circuit. How much energy is transferred by the cell?

options.text: 48 J, calculated by multiplying potential difference by charge.
3 J, calculated by dividing potential difference by charge.
16 J, calculated by adding potential difference to charge.
12 J, because a 12 V supply always gives 12 J of energy in total.

rationale: Energy transferred is calculated by multiplying potential difference by charge (W = V × Q = 12 V × 4 C = 48 J).

evidence.quote: The formula is V = W / Q, where V is the potential difference in volts (V), W is the energy in joules (J) and Q is the charge in coulombs (C).

stem: A heater in a circuit transfers 45 J of energy while 5 C of charge passes through it. What is the potential difference across the heater?

options.text: 225 V, calculated by multiplying the energy transferred by the charge.
45 V, because a battery's potential difference equals its total energy in joules.
40 V, calculated by subtracting the charge from the total energy transferred.
9 V, calculated by dividing the energy transferred by the charge.

rationale: Potential difference is calculated by dividing energy transferred by charge (V = W / Q = 45 J / 5 C = 9 V).

evidence.quote: The formula is V = W / Q, where V is the potential difference in volts (V), W is the energy in joules (J) and Q is the charge in coulombs (C).

stem: What energy transfer takes place at a bulb in a simple circuit as charge passes through it?

options.text: Energy is transferred from the charge to the surroundings as heat and light.
Energy is absorbed from surroundings by the charge as it passes through the bulb.
Energy of a fixed total amount is given to the bulb regardless of charge passed.
Energy is transferred through the circuit as potential difference flowing in wires.

rationale: A bulb acts as a component that converts energy carried by charge into heat and light transferred to the surroundings.

evidence.quote: A component such as a bulb transfers energy from the charge to its surroundings as heat and light.

stem: What happens to the resistance of a metal wire when its temperature increases?

options.text: It decreases because heating the wire causes its cross-sectional area to double.
It decreases because the thermal energy helps electric charge move through it.
It increases because vibrating atoms collide more with moving charges.
It stays exactly the same because temperature only affects voltage, not resistance.

rationale: As a metal wire gets hotter, its atoms vibrate more and collide with more of the moving charges, raising its resistance.

evidence.quote: The resistance of a metal wire rises when the wire gets hotter, because the atoms vibrate more and collide with more of the moving charge.

stem: How does the cross-sectional area of a wire affect its resistance, assuming material and length remain constant?

options.text: A thicker wire offers more resistance because it contains more material for charges to pass through.
The thickness of a wire has no effect on its resistance to electric current.
A thicker wire has a greater resistance because charge travels further across its width.
A thicker wire has a smaller resistance than a thinner wire.

rationale: A wire with a larger cross-sectional area allows current to flow more easily, resulting in smaller resistance.

evidence.quote: A thicker wire has a smaller resistance than a thinner wire of the same material and length.

stem: A metal wire of length 2 metres has a resistance of 4 Ω. What is the resistance of a wire made of the exact same material and thickness that is 6 metres long?
rationale: Because the wire is three times as long, its resistance is three times as great (3 × 4 Ω = 12 Ω).

evidence.quote: A longer wire has a greater resistance than a shorter wire of the same material and thickness.

stem: A wire with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm² has a resistance of 10 Ω. What is the resistance of a wire of the same material and length with a cross-sectional area of 2 mm²?

options.text: 5 Ω

rationale: Doubling the cross-sectional area of the wire halves its resistance, so 10 Ω is halved to 5 Ω.

evidence.quote: If the cross-sectional area is doubled, the resistance is halved.

stem: Why is copper commonly chosen for connecting wires while nichrome is used in heating elements?

options.text: Copper increases resistance when heated, whereas nichrome decreases resistance when heated.
Copper has a low resistance, whereas nichrome has a high resistance.
Copper has a high resistance, whereas nichrome has a low resistance.
Copper wire has a shorter length, whereas nichrome acts as a thicker wire.

rationale: Connecting wires require low resistance materials like copper, while heating elements require high resistance materials like nichrome.

evidence.quote: Copper has a low resistance, so it is used for connecting wires.

stem: What is the unit of measurement for electrical resistance?

options.text: Ohms (symbol Ω)
Amperes (symbol A)
Volts (symbol V)
Coulombs (symbol C)

rationale: Electrical resistance is measured in units called ohms, represented by the symbol Ω.

evidence.quote: Resistance is measured in ohms (symbol Ω).

stem: What happens to the current flowing through a component if the potential difference across it is doubled while its resistance stays constant?

options.text: It quadruples.
It drops by half.
It remains unchanged.
It doubles.

rationale: According to Ohm's law, when resistance is held constant, potential difference and current are directly proportional.

evidence.quote: When the resistance stays constant, doubling the potential difference doubles the current.

stem: According to Ohm’s law, what information is required to calculate the potential difference across a component?

options.text: You only need to know the current flowing through the component.
You must know both the current and the resistance.
You only need to know the resistance of the component.
You only need to know the total power supplied to the circuit.

rationale: Ohm's law relates potential difference, current, and resistance, meaning you must know any two quantities to calculate the third.

evidence.quote: To find any one of V, I or R, you must know the other two.

stem: A fixed potential difference is applied across a resistor with a resistance of 10 Ω, resulting in a current of 4 A. If the resistance is doubled to 20 Ω while potential difference stays constant, what is the new current?

options.text: 2 A
4 A
8 A
1 A

rationale: When the potential difference remains constant, doubling the resistance halves the current from 4 A to 2 A.

evidence.quote: When the potential difference stays constant, doubling the resistance halves the current.

stem: A component has a current of 6 A flowing through it when connected across a 12 V supply. If the potential difference is increased to 24 V while resistance remains constant, what is the new current?

options.text: 3 A
6 A

rationale: Doubling the potential difference from 12 V to 24 V at constant resistance doubles the current from 6 A to 12 A.

evidence.quote: When the resistance stays constant, doubling the potential difference doubles the current.

stem: Why is the graph of current against potential difference for a filament bulb a curve rather than a straight line?

options.text: The filament gets colder, causing its resistance to drop as current increases.
The current flowing through the filament stays constant regardless of voltage.
The potential difference can be calculated knowing only the current through it.
The filament gets hot and its resistance rises as current increases.

rationale: As current flows through a filament bulb, it heats up, raising its resistance and turning the linear relationship into a curve.

evidence.quote: The graph for a filament bulb is a curve, because the filament gets hot and its resistance rises as the current increases.

stem: Which equation correctly represents Ohm’s law?

options.text: V = I / R
I = V × R
V = R / I
V = I × R

rationale: Ohm's law defines potential difference (V) as current (I) multiplied by resistance (R).

evidence.quote: Ohm’s law states that V = I × R, where V is the potential difference in volts, I is the current in amperes and R is the resistance in ohms.

stem: What happens to the current in a series circuit when an additional resistor is added?

options.text: The current stays the same before the new resistor but decreases after passing it.
The total current remains unchanged because the cell voltage stays constant.
The total resistance increases, so the current in the circuit gets smaller.
The current in the circuit increases because extra components draw more current.

rationale: Adding a resistor increases the overall resistance of the circuit, which reduces the total current produced by the supply.

evidence.quote: Adding another resistor in series increases the total resistance, so the current in the circuit gets smaller.

stem: How is potential difference shared across components with different resistances connected in series?

options.text: The component with the larger resistance gets the larger share of the potential difference.
The component with the smaller resistance gets the larger share of the potential difference.
Both components receive equal potential difference regardless of their resistance values.
The first component uses up most of the current, leaving less voltage for the second.

rationale: In a series circuit, potential difference is divided across components in proportion to their resistance, so higher resistance gets a larger voltage share.

evidence.quote: If the resistances are different, the component with the larger resistance gets the larger share of the potential difference.

stem: A 15 V cell is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the 3 Ω resistor?

options.text: 6 V
3 V
9 V

rationale: The total resistance is 5 Ω, giving a circuit current of 3 A (15 V / 5 Ω), so the potential difference across the 3 Ω resistor is 3 A × 3 Ω = 9 V.

evidence.quote: The potential differences across the components add up to the potential difference of the supply: V total = V1 + V2 + V3.

stem: An ammeter placed before a bulb in a series circuit reads 0.4 A. What will an ammeter placed immediately after the bulb read?

options.text: 0.4 A, because current is the same at every point in a series circuit.
0.8 A, because adding a bulb causes the circuit current to increase.
0.2 A, because electric current gets used up as it flows through the bulb.
0.0 A, because current is entirely converted into heat and light.

rationale: Electric current is not consumed as it passes through components, so the current reading is identical everywhere in a series loop.

evidence.quote: An ammeter placed before, between or after the components of a series circuit shows the same reading.

stem: How is the total resistance calculated when multiple components are connected in series?

options.text: By adding resistors, which causes the current in the circuit to increase.
By multiplying all of the individual component resistances together.
By dividing the supply voltage by the total number of components.
By calculating the sum of the individual resistances of all components.

rationale: The combined opposition to current in a single path is equal to the sum of each component's individual resistance.

evidence.quote: The total resistance of components in series is the sum of their resistances: R total = R1 + R2 + R3.

stem: Why is there only one path for electric charge in a series circuit?

options.text: Because potential difference pushes current through only one path at a time.
Because current gets used up gradually as it flows through components.
Because the components are connected end-to-end in a single loop.
Because adding extra resistors causes the circuit current to increase rapidly.

rationale: In a series circuit, components are connected sequentially to form a single continuous pathway for the charge.

evidence.quote: In a series circuit there is only one path for the charge.
